references.text: Isaiah describes the Lord's servant who gives his back to those who strike him and his cheeks to those who pull out his beard – a prophetic parallel to Jesus' teaching about turning the other cheek.
Lamentations urges one to turn the cheek to the striker and bear shame patiently – the same motif found in Luke 6:29.
Matthew's parallel passage to Jesus' teaching on turning the other cheek and giving up your cloak, from the Sermon on the Mount. This is the closest parallel to Luke 6:29.
Paul exhorts believers not to repay evil with evil but to overcome evil with good – a practical application of the principle Jesus teaches in Luke 6:29.
Paul asks the Corinthians why they do not rather suffer wrong and endure loss than go to court against one another – the same principle of enduring injustice that Jesus teaches.
Peter urges believers to endure unjust suffering patiently, pointing to Christ as an example – he who did not repay when he was insulted or suffered.
Peter exhorts them not to repay evil with evil or insult with insult but rather to bless – reflecting Jesus' teaching about turning the other cheek.
Proverbs warns against saying 'I will repay evil,' and urges waiting on the Lord – a wisdom saying that points toward Jesus' radical teaching of non-retaliation.
Proverbs warns against saying 'As he has done to me, so I will do to him' – a principle that Jesus radicalizes in his teaching about turning the other cheek.
